yt.title: MOSFET Numericals | Square Law, Biasing, Saturation Check, Gain - Solved | Analog Electronics
yt.description: Five MOSFET problems solved step by step with the circuit on screen: drain current from the square law, a fixed gate bias with VDS and the saturation check, voltage-divider bias with a source resistor solved by the quadratic, transconductance and voltage gain, and an ohmic-region switching check with RDS(on).

scenes.title: MOSFET NUMERICALS
scenes.subtitle: Five problems, solved step by step
scenes.narration: Welcome back. Practice time for MOSFETs. Five problems, each solved one step at a time. All use an N channel enhancement MOSFET with a threshold of two volts and k of zero point five milliamps per volt squared, on a twelve volt supply. Pause and try each one first.

Problem one. V G S is five volts. Find I D in saturation. I D equals k times V G S minus V T, squared: zero point five milliamps times five minus two, squared, zero point five times nine, four point five milliamps.
lines: VGS = 5 V, VT = 2 V, k = 0.5 mA/V²

scenes.chapter: Problem 2: VDS and the saturation check
scenes.narration: Problem two. Same five volts on the gate, R D one point five k, no source resistor. Find V D S and check the region. V D S equals twelve minus four point five milliamps times one point five k: twelve minus six point seven five, five point two five volts. Saturation needs V D S at least V G S minus V T, three volts. Five point two five is more than three, so it's saturated, and the answer is valid.

Problem three. Our biased amplifier: gate divider two megohms and one megohm, R S one k, R D six point eight k. V G is four volts. V G S equals four minus I D times one k. Substitute: I D equals zero point five milliamps times two minus one k I D, squared. Expand into a quadratic. In milliamps: I D squared minus six I D plus four equals zero. The roots are five point two four and zero point seven six four milliamps. The first would make V G S negative, below threshold, so it's impossible. I D is zero point seven six four milliamps.

Problem four. For problem three, find g m and the gain with the source resistor bypassed. g m equals two k times V G S minus V T: two times zero point five milliamps times one point two four, one point two four milliamps per volt. Gain equals minus g m times R D: minus one point two four milliamps times six point eight k, minus eight point four. Without the bypass capacitor, gain is minus g m R D over one plus g m R S: minus eight point four over two point two four, minus three point seven five.
lines: no bypass: Av = −gm RD ÷ (1 + gm RS)

scenes.narration: Problem five. A MOSFET with R D S on of zero point zero five ohms switches a twelve ohm load from twelve volts. Find the current and the MOSFET's heat. The current is twelve over twelve point zero five, essentially one amp. The voltage across the MOSFET: one amp times zero point zero five, fifty millivolts. Heat: one squared times zero point zero five, zero point zero five watts. In the ohmic region, the square law doesn't apply. Use R D S on.

The mistakes that cost marks. One: picking the wrong root of the quadratic. Always check that V G S is above V T. Two: skipping the saturation check: V D S at least V G S minus V T. Three: using the square law for a MOSFET used as a switch. There, it's in the ohmic region, so use R D S on.
lines: ✓ pick the root with VGS > VT
✓ switch → use RDS(on), not the square law

scenes.title: NEXT: CMOS INVERTER
lines: Quadratic: keep the root with VGS > VT
scenes.narration: Quick recap. Use the square law in saturation, check V D S is at least V G S minus V T, pick the quadratic root with V G S above threshold, and use g m equals two k times V G S minus V T for the gain. Next, the circuit built from two MOSFETs that powers every computer: the C M O S inverter. See you there.
